extracted.intended_audience: regulated entities, employers, legal counsel, policymakers, and members of the public participating in FTC rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and legal/empirical standards the Federal Trade Commission uses to justify and promulgate a rule addressing employer use of non-compete clauses, including findings about prevalence, statutory authority under sections 5 and 6(g), evidentiary evaluation, and procedural/regulatory-analysis obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of Non-Competes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds that non-competes are in widespread use throughout the economy and pervasive across industries and demographic groups; it estimates approximately one in five American workers—or approximately 30 million workers—is subject to a non-compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission bases this finding on its own data analysis, studies published by economists, and the comment record. Multiple surveys and studies (2014 worker survey, NLSY-based 2022 study, Federal Reserve survey, industry-specific surveys, and commenter-provided data) are cited; the Commission also acknowledges heterogeneity across industries and demographics but treats the prevalence as sufficient to support broad coverage under the rule. A finding of prevalence is not necessary to support a section 5 determination, but prevalence corroborates observed negative effects on competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry Under Section 5 Focuses on Nature and Tendency of Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry as to whether conduct is an unfair method of competition under section 5 focuses on the nature and tendency of the conduct, not whether or to what degree the conduct caused actual harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission evaluates whether the conduct tends to stifle or impair competition; actual measured harm is not required. This standard allows the Commission to address practices that can foreseeably impair competition even if specific quantified harms are contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Multiple Evidence Streams
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission relies on a combination of its own data analysis, published academic studies, and the public comment record to reach findings supporting the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission draws on a variety of studies (surveys, NLSY analyses, occupation-specific studies) and commenter submissions. It gives weight to representative studies and corroborating commenter data, but it also explains limitations where studies are nonrepresentative or lack methodological detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of Survey Methodology and Credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys and commenter-submitted estimates are assessed for methodological rigor; convenience samples and studies lacking underlying data or methodology are treated with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission notes specific methodological limitations (e.g., convenience samples like Payscale.com visitors), explains that weighting helps but does not eliminate concerns, and disfavors relying solely on surveys without accessible methodology or raw data. Commenter-provided surveys without methods are not relied upon to the same degree as well-documented academic studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Occupation- and Industry-Specific Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission reviews occupation- and industry-specific prevalence data and commenter evidence about non-compete use across professions (e.g., physicians, engineers, hair stylists, executives), but finds heterogeneity insufficient to require industry-specific exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although prevalence varies by industry and occupation, that heterogeneity does not alone justify exempting sectors from the rule because non-competes are nonetheless widespread across labor markets and because other parts of the rulemaking record (e.g., harms) support broad coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission's Legal Authority under Sections 5 and 6(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plain text of sections 5 and 6(g) of the FTC Act empower the Commission to promulgate rules to prevent unfair methods of competition, including legislative rules defining certain conduct as an unfair method of competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission supports this view with historical practice, prior rulemakings under section 6(g), and appellate decisions (e.g., Petroleum Refiners) upholding its authority. Congress's later amendments (1975, 1980) preserved and evidenced awareness of that authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical Precedent of Substantive Rulemaking Under Section 6(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission may (and historically has) promulgated substantive rules under section 6(g) that declare particular practices to be unfair methods of competition or unfair/deceptive acts or practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble lists many concrete historical rulemakings (e.g., Octane Rule, Unavailability Rule, Mail Order Rule, Cigarette Rule) as precedent supporting the Commission's authority to issue rules that define unlawful conduct under section 6(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction Between Section 6(g) and Section 18/UDAP Rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Congress enacted section 18 (1975) and imposed new procedures for UDAP rules, it expressly preserved the Commission's authority under section 6(g) to promulgate rules addressing unfair methods of competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission interprets legislative history and statutory text to mean that Congress intended to limit UDAP rulemaking procedures but did not remove section 6(g) authority to regulate unfair methods of competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to Agency Expertise in Determining Unfair Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts reviewing Commission determinations historically give the Commission's decisions 'great weight' as an expert agency in making determinations about anticompetitive conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission relies on judicial recognition of its expert role and past judicial deference when construing the scope of section 5 and the Commission's rulemaking authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Remedies Under Section 5
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Commission can pursue adjudications under section 5(b) or seek injunctions in federal court under section 13(b), the Commission cannot generally obtain civil penalties or other monetary relief from parties who engage in an unfair method of competition, except in certain enforcement scenarios (e.g., penalties for failure to comply with a cease and desist order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural limitation informs the form of relief the Commission expects to seek and communicate in the rulemaking and enforcement context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 22 and Regulatory Analysis Obligations for Significant Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 22 contemplates that certain rules will require regulatory analysis obligations (cost-benefit analysis, assessment of substantial economic effects) when rules 'have an annual effect on the national economy of $100,000,000 or more' or otherwise have significant impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission acknowledges the procedural and analytical obligations in section 22 and treats them as consistent with its authority to issue economically significant legislative rules under section 6(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing Common Commenter Legal Arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission catalogs and responds to common legal objections raised by commenters: (1) the FTC Act does not grant authority to promulgate the rule; (2) the issue is a 'major question' reserved to Congress; (3) Congress impermissibly delegated nationwide rulemaking authority to the Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each objection the Commission explains why it disagrees, grounding its response in statutory text, legislative history, precedent, and the structure of the Act, and explains that the final rule will apply only to the extent of the Commission's jurisdiction under the FTC Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Broad, Flexible Statutory Language
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'unfair methods of competition' was deliberately adopted as a broader and more flexible phrase than the common law notion of 'unfair competition,' and Congress intentionally left its scope imprecise to allow the Commission to adapt to changing circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretive posture permits the Commission to address novel or evolving practices (like widespread non-competes) that may impair competition even if not precisely foreseen when the statute was enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Anecdotal and Individual Commenter Experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission reviews and incorporates individual comment submissions describing harms from non-competes (e.g., personal stories from physicians, bartenders, veterinarians, small business owners, laid-off workers) as illustrative of harms to workers, patients, clients, and entrepreneurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While recognizing limitations of anecdotal evidence, the Commission uses these narratives in the rulemaking record to illustrate real-world consequences and patterns that complement quantitative studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility Assessment of Trade Association and Employer Surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission evaluates surveys submitted by trade organizations and associations (e.g., HR Policy Association, Retail Industry Leaders Association) for representativeness and underlying data; where methodology or data are not provided, claims may be given less weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some industry commenters reported lower usage rates based on proprietary surveys without underlying data; the Commission notes these limitations and does not rely solely on them to overturn the broader body of evidence.
